title: SCAPULA BRACE
abstract: A medical device (100) for treatment or prevention of the subacromial pain syndrome of a living object is described. The medical device (100) comprises a means for exerting pressure (110) on a scapula and/or clavicle/acromion for rotating the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion in a posteriorly tilted position, and a means for providing a counter force (130) so the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion can be maintained in the posteriorly tilted position.

description: Scapula Brace Field of the invention The invention relates to devices for assisting in physiotherapy. More particularly, the present invention provides devices for assisting in physiotherapy for overcoming the subacromial pain syndrome. Background of the invention The shoulder is a complex joint. Since this is the most agile joint in the human body, it can suffer from a variety of problems that are not often easy to deal with. One of the most common shoulder complaints is the subacromial pain syndrome. About 40 percent of the shoulder complaints are due to a subacromial pain syndrome. Subacromial pain syndrome is often thought to be caused by the reduction of the space between the humerus, the upper arm bone and the scapula. Normally there is sufficient space between between the acromion, the processus coracoideus and the tubercle major (shoulder blade and upper arm bone) so that the tendon positioned in this space can sufficiently move. If this space under the acromion nevertheless becomes smaller, the tendon can come into contact with the acromion, which can cause irritation and inflammation. This in turn can lead to pain, mainly when lifting the arm above 60 degrees or when moving the arm backwards. One of the possible causes for reduction of the space at the acromion is a deviation of the scapula, also referred to as scapular dyskinesis. This abnormality of the scapula can occur because the front pectoral muscle, also referred to as minor pectoralis, is greatly shortened, for example by too much training. The back muscles, also referred to as the trapezius muscles, should in principle be equally long and equally strong, but they become weaker and longer due to overtraining. As a result, the scapula will be pulled forward and tilted. This position may compromise the subacromial space or at least put the rotator cuff muscles in a difficult length tension relationship in order to properly function. This can be treated through stretching and exercises. The target group suffering most from subacromial pain syndrome can be divided into three groups. The first group are the so-called overhead athletes. These are athletes who exercise a sport in which a lot is moved with the hands above the head. Just think of all kinds of throwing sports, such as baseball, javelin throw, handball, ... as well as on volleyball, basketball, tennis and swimming. A subacromial pain syndrome can occur for both professional and recreational athletes and is, as mentioned earlier, due to e.g. over-training of the pectoral muscle. A second group are workers who often have to perform movements similar to these performed by athletes. Especially for work where hands are to be moved above the head, this may introduce the problem. One example thereof are painters. A subacromial pain syndrome can also occur with less active people. Then it usually comes from performing extreme movements. For example, people who are sitting behind a desk all day, but who go to work in the garden once in the weekend or start a sport once. Here too, this subacromial pain syndrome can suddenly occur. The treatments for the different target groups are the same. Currently the diagnosis is usually determined by a doctor who then refers the patient to the physiotherapist. The physiotherapist will further investigate what kind of subacromial pain syndrome is involved by means of a few tests. If scapular dyskinesis is noted and related to the patients' shoulder pain, he will start treatment for this. This is currently a based-on exercises therapy, assisted by manual therapy, in which he will stretch the chest muscles in the patient and teach the patient to keep his own shoulder blade in this position. When the patient can hold the scapula in the correct position in passive condition, he continues to learn how to do this in active condition during movement. The patient typically visits the physiotherapist two or three times a week to do these exercises. This is a time-consuming and costly therapy. Summary of the invention It is an object of embodiments of the present invention to provide a good system for assisting in physiotherapy for treatment of or prevention of the subacromial pain syndrome, as well as a corresponding method and software for controlling the system. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the medical device allows to reduce the number of consultancies to the physiotherapist, thus providing additional time for the patient as well as introducing a cost reduction. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the systems are comfortable to wear and to use. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the stretching required for overcoming or preventing the subacromial pain syndrome can be provided by the medical device. The latter is obtained by putting a pressure on the bottom of the scapula so that it returns to its original position. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the medical device, also referred to as orthopedic device, can used for prevention of injuries as well as for therapy. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the medical device, amongst which the pressure inducing means, can be compact and simple. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the weight of the tilting mechanism is relatively small. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the systems are easy to use, e.g. so that clothes can still be worn. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the system is simple in structure, so that it does not occupy too much space, as well as in use. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the altitude can be set both the physiotherapist and the user, and that the pressure can be easily controlled or set by the physiotherapist. The object is overcome by a system and method according to embodiments of the present invention. The present invention relates to a medical device for treatment or prevention of the subacromial pain syndrome of a living object. The medical device comprises a means for exerting pressure on a scapula and/or clavicle/acromion for rotating the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion in a posteriorly tilted position. The medical device also comprises a means for providing a counter force so the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion can be maintained in the posteriorly tilted position. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the medical device allows that the subacromial space of the living object can be enlarged or re enlarged and that the rotator cuff is given a better length-tension relationship, thus allowing to treat or avoid subacromial pain syndrome. In this way, the rotator cuff is given a more stable base for optimized functioning. The means for exerting pressure may be an adjustable means for exerting pressure adapted for adjusting the pressure applied on the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the medical device can be adapted to the individual patient level. The means for exerting pressure may be adapted for mechanically adjusting the pressure applied on the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the medical device can be easily manufactured and that conventional mechanical means, such as for example spring based elements, can be used for controlling the amount of pressure applied. The means for exerting pressure may be adapted for electronically adjusting the pressure applied on the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the medical device, and more particularly the amount of pressure that is applied, can be controlled by various inputs, e.g. in function of recovery, prevention, pain or discomfort, or by a physiotherapist from a distance, so that the medical device can be adapted without the need for explicit intervention, e.g. by touching the device. The device furthermore may comprise a controller and wherein the controller is programmed for automatically adjusting the means for exerting pressure as function of the therapy stage. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the operation of the medical device can be automatically adjusted as function of the therapy stage, or specific situation were prevention is desired, such that the appropriate operation can be guaranteed at all moments in time during the therapy or prevention stage. The device furthermore may comprise one or more force sensors or force sensing textile for sensing a force applied to the living object by the device. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the effective pressure applied to the living object, taking into account the specific situation and physical characteristics of the living object, e.g. patient, can be measured. The medical device may comprise a brace portion around the shoulder and a waistband for connecting to a patient's waste, the device further comprising a connection between the brace portion and the waistband. The brace portion and the waistband may be connected via a belt with a belt tensioner. The brace portion and the waistband may be connected via a rigid element. At least one sensor is positioned at the clavicle/acromion for sensing pressure on the clavicle and/or acromion. At least one sensor is positioned on the patients back for deriving a rotational force on the scapula. The medical device may comprise a brace at the shoulder and a waistband and the sensor may be positioned between the brace and the waistband. At least one sensor may be positioned at the back of the scapula. The one or more force sensors or force sensing textile may be configured in position for sensing the force applied at the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion. The controller may be programmed for receiving an input from the one or more force sensors and wherein the controller is programmed for controlling the exerted pressure as function of the sensed force. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the applied pressure takes into account instantaneous force measurements, such that the applied pressure corresponds with the actual situation. The controller may be programmed for controlling the exerted pressure to be constant, as function of the preferred therapy or action. The means for providing a counter force may be a brace for fixating the device to the body of the living object. The means for providing a counter force may be bands for fixating the device to the body of the living object. The means for providing a counter force may be a textile. It is an advantage of embodiments of the present invention that the medical device can be embodied in a sleeve or shirt or backpack to be worn by the living object. The controller can be driven by a user using a computer application, installed for example on a mobile device. The medical device may comprise a processor for controlling the applied pressure based on an algorithm, on a neural network or on a database comprising former knowledge on pressure- therapy effects. The device may be implemented in a garment or a backpack. The present invention also relates to a computer program product, the computer program product being adapted for, when executed on a processor of the medical device as described above, obtaining a force applied to the living object by the medical device and controlling the exerted pressure as function of the sensed force so as to keep the force substantially constant at a predetermined value depending on the preferred therapy or preferred exercising program. The present invention also relates to the use of a medical device as described above for the treatment of subacromial pain syndrome as well as the use of a medical device as described above for preventing subacromial pain syndrome. In a first aspect, the present invention relates to a medical device for treatment or prevention of the subacromial pain syndrome of a living object is described. The medical device comprises a means for exerting pressure on a scapula and/or clavicle/acromion for rotating the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion in a posteriorly tilted position, and a means for providing a counter force so the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion can be maintained in the posteriorly tilted position. By way of illustration, embodiments of the present invention not being limited thereto, an exemplary embodiment of a medical device according to the present invention will be described below with reference to drawings FIG. 1 to FIG. 11. FIG. 1 to FIG. 4 and FIG. 6 to FIG. 8 show different views on the medical device 100 according to the exemplary embodiment. The medical device 100 comprises a means for exerting pressure 110 on a scapula and/or clavicle/acromion. This means for exerting pressure is adapted so that, in operation, it rotates the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion in a posteriorly tilted position. The medical device thus is adapted for rotating the scapula, that is in the case of scapular dyskinesis pulled forward and tilted, back into its normal position. The means for exerting pressure 110 may, as in the example shown, comprises pressure pads 112, 114 for transferring pressure from the means for exerting pressure 110 to the body of the living being. The pressure pads 112, 114 may comprise a first pressure pad 112 adapted for applying pressure at the front side of the shoulder (i.e. the front side of the patient) and a second pressure pad 114 adapted for applying pressure at the back side of the shoulder. The first pressure pad 112 and the second pressure pad 114 may be adapted for inducing a rotation of the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion in a posteriorly tilted position. The first pressure pad 112 providing pressure at a front side of the scapula may be positioned higher than the second pressure pad 114 providing pressure at a back side of the scapula (with respect to the upstanding patient). The pressure pads may in some embodiments be pressure plates. These pressure plates may be made of any suitable materials, such as plastics, a metal or a carbon fiber based material. The means for exerting pressure 110 to the body of the living being typically also comprises at least one force inducing element, such as for example a spring, a settable hinge or any other suitable force inducing element, e.g. textile, shape and physical properties can be obtained by 3D knitting. In the exemplary embodiment, a first force inducing element 116 is provided for applying a force on the first pressure pad 112 and a second force inducing element 118 is provided for applying a force on the second pressure pad 114 so that the scapula is rotated into a posteriorly tilted position. In this way, the scapula which e.g. in the case of scapular dyskinesis is pulled forward and tilted, is forced back into its posteriorly tilted position. Alternatively, if the orthopedic device is not used for the case of scapular dyskinesis but for preventing the occurrence of scapular dyskinesis, the scapula can be prevented from being pulled forward and tilted by application of the orthopedic device. The motion implemented on the scapula is illustrated in FIG. 5 and FIG. 11, whereby in FIG. 11 the direction of tilting is shown. The at least one force inducing element may be controllable such that the amount of pressure applied can be controlled. Such controllability may allow to set the applied pressure to values corresponding with those as applied when performing manual treatment. Reporting of the typically applied forces can for example be found in "Effects of scapular dyskinesis and scapular assistance test on subacromial space during static arm elevation." by Seitz AL et al. in J. Shoulder Elbow Surg. (2012) 21 (5) pp631-40, reporting on forces applied during manual treatment. The effect of the applied therapy, in the case of manual application as known from prior art, is described in "Effect of the Scapula Reposition Test on shoulder impingement symptoms and elevation strength in overhead athletes" by Tate AR et al. in J. Orthop. Sports Phys. Ther. (2008) 38(1) pp 4-11. The at least one force inducing element may for example be settable with respect to the force that is applied using setting screws or, in some embodiments where one or more hinges are used, using a particular configuration of the hinge used. In some embodiments, the force to be applied may be settable manually. In other embodiments, the force to be applied by the at least one force inducing element may be settable in an automated way, so that the force applied by the at least one force inducing element can be controlled from a distance. In some embodiments, the medical device also may comprise sensors for sensing a pressure that is applied by the medical device on the patient / user. The system can in this way also comprise a feedback system for providing feedback with respect to the pressure that is applied. The system may be adapted for automatically adjusting the force applied by the at least one force inducing element, such that the pressure applied by the medical device on the patient /user is at a predetermined value. In some embodiment, one pressure sensor is applied at the clavicle/acromion for sensing whether there is too much pressure on it, since the acromion is a sensitive part of the human body. This sensor can be a simple load cell or it can eventually be made from force sensing textile. It will be understood that also other pressure sensor could be used for sensing at the clavicle/acromion. This sensor can be combined with other sensors. In some embodiments, a sensor is applied on the patients back, between a brace portion and a waistband connected to each other. Such a brace portion and waistband may in general be present in other embodiments of the present invention, not comprising the force sensor. This sensor is a (pulling-)force sensor. Such a sensor may be configured for reading out, managing and/or optimizing the tension from the adjustable waist band. This tension may advantageously be optimised, since this tension will evoke the rotational force (momentum) needed to reposition the scapula. This sensor can be a load cell or a force sensing textile as well. It will be understood that also other sensors could be used. This sensor can be combined with other sensors. In some embodiments, a sensor positioned at the back of the scapula is provided. This sensor can be combined with other sensors. In some embodiments, the medical device comprises a controller for controlling the force applied. The controller may be programmed for obtaining a pressure applied to the patient / user by the medical device and for controlling the exerted pressure as function of the sensed force so as to keep the force substantially constant at a predetermined value depending on the preferred therapy or preferred exercising program. The controller may make use of an algorithm, a neural network or a look up table for determining the force, typically a constant force selected as function of the therapy or exercise that is selected for the patient/user, to be applied. In some other embodiments, the controller also may be configured for automatically adjusting the pressure applied to the scapula over time. The controller may be configured for, according to a certain therapy or exercise one wishes to apply, automatically adjusting the applied pressure by the medical device over time. The controller therefore may be adapted for storing predetermined settings in line with a therapy or exercise to be applied over time. Alternatively, the controller also may be adapted for being remotely driven, e.g. based on the input of a physiotherapist. The means for exerting a pressure also may comprise a brace 120 to which the pressure pads and the force inducing means are connected. Such a brace may be adjustable to the patient/user or may be custom made for the patient /user. The brace may be made of any suitable material, such as for example a metal based brace covered with a polyurethane layer, to increase patient comfort. The materials used to make the brace may in some embodiments be aluminum. The materials used to make the brace may in some embodiments be a plastic, such as for example PE or PP. In yet another alternative embodiment, the brace may be made of a carbon fiber based material. The brace 120 may be adjustable to the patient / user. The position of the pressure pads 112, 114 with respect to the brace 120 may be adjustable, such that an accurate position of the pressure pad with respect to the human body is selectable. Especially the height of the pressure pads with respect to the patient / user may be selectable. Different techniques may be used for positioning the pressure pads with respect to the brace such as for example based on Velcro or another fixation means. The medical device 100 also comprises a means for providing a counter force 130 so the scapula and/or clavicle/acromion can be maintained in the posteriorly tilted position. The means for providing a counter force 130 may be a brace for fixating the device to the body of the living object. In alternative embodiments, the means for providing a counter force 130 may be bands for fixating the device to the body of the living object. In yet other embodiments, the means for providing a counter force 130 may be a textile. It may for example be a garment or it may be a backpack. The medical device 100 may itself be implemented as a garment or a backpack. FIG. 9 and FIG. 10 illustrate how the medical device 100 can be worn by a patient. The present invention also relates to a computer program product for controlling the medical device. The computer program product according to embodiments of the present invention is adapted for, when executed on a processor of the medical device as described in the first aspect, performing obtaining a force applied to the living object by the medical device and controlling the exerted pressure as function of the sensed force so as to keep the force substantially constant at a predetermined value depending on the preferred therapy or preferred exercising program. The computer program product may make use of an algorithm, a neural network or a look up table for determining the force, typically a constant force selected as function of the therapy or exercise that is selected for the patient/user, to be applied. Further by way of illustration, another configuration of a medical device 100 according to an embodiment of the present invention is illustrated from different views in FIG. 12 to FIG. 16. In FIG. 16, by way of illustration and embodiments not being limited thereto, the medical device 100 is shown illustrating a brace portion 200, a force sensor 202, a belt tensioner 204 and a waistband 206. In some embodiments, the medical device thus comprises a brace portion and a waistband, which typically may be connected with each other. Such a connection may be performed by means of a belt. On the belt, a belt tensioner may be present for controlling the tension implied by the belt. The force applied may be measured by a force sensor. In some more advanced devices, a controller may control the force applied by controlling based on a measured force the belt tensioner. In some embodiments, the medical device may comprises instead of or in addition to a belt connection between the waistband and the brace, a rigid connection, such as for example a bar connection. If the rigid connection is provided in combination with the tension belt, the tension belt may be used for applying a larger moment to the shoulder. The tension belt then may be connected above the rigid connection, one example thereof being illustrated in FIG. 17. The use of the rigid connection may result in a reduced load on the back, an accurate determination of the rotation point for the moment applied , the scapula being pushed upwardly and being rotated in the correct position and/or a reduced risk of shift in the waistband. By way of illustration, embodiments of the present invention not being limited thereto, an illustration of the forces that act, as currently understood is, is given below. The one or more sensors applied can advantageously be used for deriving or indicating size/direction of one or more of these forces and/or may be used as a basis for adjusting the applied forces. The main forces in the medical device can be represented by three pairs of forces. The force in the tension belt connecting the brace portion and the waistband, as indicated in FIG. 18 by force FI and the corresponding moment Ml imposed, the pressure applied by the brace portion on the body as indicated by PI and P2, and the frictional force of the brace on the body, indicated by Fwrl and Fwr2. The three force pairs each influence each other. Force FI could be considered the most relevant, since positioning of the scapula may be mostly determined by the point of rotation and the moment that is applied to the Force FI. The latter is illustrated in FIG. 19. The point of rotation Ό' now is positioned close to the position of the pressure sensor at the back of the scapula, if such pressure sensor is present. In order to determine the size of the moment Ml, both the force FI applied and an estimate of the perpendicular distance between FI and the rotation point needs to be known. The medical device may be adapted for providing information regarding the moment, based on the force FI, e.g. sensed with a sensor sensing the pulling force, and based on a user input or measurement of the distance r. The size of the pressure PI and P2 could also be monitored using one or more pressure sensors, as described above. These may give an indication of pressures that provide an allowable, e.g. comfortable, pressure for the patient. This may allow avoiding injuries or pain. The present invention also relates to a method for using a medical device as described in the first aspect for performing in physiotherapy for overcoming the subacromial pain syndrome. The method may include using the medical device, sensing an applied pressure and controlling the medical device such that a predetermined pressure is applied. The predetermined pressure may be according to values that are determined by the physiotherapist. In some embodiments, the method also includes the automated adjusting of the medical device, or more particularly the pressure applied to the scapula, in order to provide therapy or exercises that are dynamic over time, i.e. that provide a different pressure to the scapula as function of the stage of the therapy or exercise. Further method steps may correspond with the functionality of the features of the medical device as described in the first aspect. By way of illustration, embodiments of the present invention not being limited to it, a study of 13 patients was held, the patients having limited complaints regarding shoulder pain. Two questionnaires were used for evaluating whether the scapula brace device according to an embodiment of the present invention could bring forward a significant reduction of complaints for the patient. The first questionnaire is the Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI) questionnaire and the second questionnaire is the Disability of Shoulder and Hand (DASH) questionnaire. Both questionnaires comprise a combination of pain related questions and restriction-related questions. The study showed that patient experience a statistically significant decrease of pain complaints after applying the scapula device (for SPADI questions related to pain, the score is significantly lower, i.e. (t-test : p < 0.05)). The effects evaluated were effects on short term.
